cases.title: New Flour Trial
cases.setting: You run a small bakery. In April you switched your sourdough loaf to a new flour, hoping to cut customer complaints, which had been running at about 9 a week. You published a claim about the new flour and fixed your commitment before any of the six trial weeks were counted. The counts are now in.
cases.claim: With the new flour, complaints about the sourdough loaf fall to fewer than 3 a week in every one of the six trial weeks.

commitment.falsifier: Any trial week with 3 or more complaints defeats the claim.
forbidden: Any change, once the figures are in, to what is counted, where the line sits, or what the claim covers.

evidence: Weekly complaint counts over the six weeks were 2, 6, 7, 2, 5 and 1; four of the six weeks reached 3 or more.
Every complaint was logged in the same book, at the same counter and for the same sourdough loaf as before the change; weeks 2, 3 and 5 fell during the town's summer fair.
The taste-panel score planned for week 4 could not be evaluated: the panel's score sheet was mislaid and has not been found.
Loaf weight, checked daily, stayed within 10 grams of target in all six weeks, as it did on the old flour.

moves.text: I mark the claim rejected, the consequence fixed in advance, and write the date, the six weekly counts and the change beside the original claim on the shop notice board.
I set aside weeks 2, 3 and 5, the three fair weeks that produced the failing counts, and tally the remaining three weeks, which all come in under 3.
I count the mislaid taste-panel sheet as a failure and, on that basis, withdraw my separate claim that the new flour tastes no different from the old.
I withdraw the claim and record instead what the six weeks showed, 2, 6, 7, 2, 5 and 1 complaints a week; a recount of the same book giving other figures would overturn it.
I set the weekly limit at under 8 in place of under 3 and read the six counts against that line, under which every one of the weeks passes.
I withdraw the new flour from every bread we make, retract the loaf-weight result with it, and return the whole shop to the old supplier from next week.
I count the six weeks a second time from the same book, same limit, same loaf, exactly as I would have for a good result, and record whichever figures the second count gives.
I read the claim as one about our regular weekday customers, whose complaints stayed under 3 in every week, and record that on that reading the claim stands.

cases.title: Route 4 Timetable
cases.setting: You manage a small town bus depot. In March you moved route 4 from every 20 minutes to every 15 in the morning peak, to stop buses arriving late; before the change about 30 percent of peak arrivals were more than five minutes late. You published a claim and fixed your commitment before the first four weeks were counted. The figures are now in.
cases.claim: On the 15-minute timetable, fewer than 10 percent of morning-peak arrivals on route 4 are more than five minutes late in each of the first four weeks.

commitment.falsifier: Any of the four weeks with a late share above 10 percent defeats the claim.
forbidden: Any change, once the figures are in, to what is counted, where the line sits, or what the claim covers.

evidence: The planned check of driver duty sheets for week 2 could not be evaluated: the depot's copies went to head office and were not returned.
Passenger numbers on route 4, counted by the same machines, rose 12 percent against the previous month; the claim did not rest on this figure.
The weekly late shares were 8, 17, 21 and 14 percent; three of the four weeks were above 10 percent.
All counts come from the same ticket-machine clock and the same twelve stops used before the change; six roadworks days across weeks 2, 3 and 4 hold most of the late arrivals.

moves.text: I have the four weeks recounted on the same twelve stops, peak hour, five-minute line and machine clock, the step I take for a good result too, and I record whatever the recount gives.
I restate the claim as covering the town-centre stops, where the late share stayed under 10 percent in each week, and keep it published in that form.
I pull the 15-minute timetable, strike the 12 percent passenger figure from the record, and put every route at the depot back on its old frequency from Monday.
I record the claim as rejected, the outcome fixed for it beforehand, and enter the date, the four late-share percentages and the change on the depot notice next to the original wording.
I take ten minutes rather than five as the line for a late arrival and reread the four weeks against it, which brings each week below 10 percent.
I log the unreturned duty sheets as a failed check, and on the strength of that entry I withdraw my separate claim about drivers keeping their planned rest breaks.
I withdraw the published claim and put in its place the four measured late shares, 8, 17, 21 and 14 percent; a fresh reading of the same machine records that differs would overturn it.
I remove the six roadworks days, the days carrying the late arrivals that failed the claim, from the count and report each week on its remaining days, all under 10 percent.
